clue.text: Hangers-on seen off by local manager

parts.note: lice are parasites that cling on to their host, so they are hangers-on

indicators.note: off here means gone wrong, so the letters of seen are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pub's landlord sends the freeloaders packing.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'local' in Britain is a neighbourhood pub, and its manager holds the licence to sell drink; 'off' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The holder of a pub's drinks licence runs the local, so the publican is called by that title.

clue.text: See 5
Exhausts cause supercharger's casing to drop off

indicators.note: letting the outer letters fall away leaves the run of letters inside the words cause supercharger

explanation.surface: A mechanic explains that losing the outer shell of the supercharger makes the engine run out of puff.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits inside caUSE SUPercharger once the casing letters on each side are dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust a supply is to consume it entirely, the phrasal verb meaning the same.

clue.text: Blue liquid ready to be applied

indicators.note: liquid means flowing and unfixed, so the letters of Blue are allowed to run into a new order

explanation.surface: A blue fluid is primed for application.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid' rearranges Blue; the preamble's theme word SEA, which the wordplay never supplies, is then slotted in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fit for use is in a state where it can be put to work, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Bloomer made by Scottish team at bottom of table

parts.note: Hearts, Heart of Midlothian, is an Edinburgh football club

indicators.note: the bottom of a word written downwards is its last letter, so the end of table

explanation.surface: A Scottish football side props up the league and makes a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a gaffe, but it is a flower. Hearts is an Edinburgh football club; the theme word SEA is slotted in after its fifth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This wild pansy is a flower, and a bloomer is crossword shorthand for anything that blooms.

clue.text: Naval apprentice upset initially by this?

definitions.text: Naval apprentice upset initially by this?

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of the three words before it

parts.note: the preamble's three-letter word, absent from the wordplay and added to every themed answer

explanation.surface: A trainee sailor is thrown off balance, perhaps by seasickness.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters give NAU and the theme word SEA completes it. The whole clue also describes a queasy young sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Sickness at sea is exactly what upsets a fresh naval recruit's stomach.

clue.text: Side's phoney complaints

indicators.note: phoney means fake, so the letters are rearranged into a counterfeit order

parts.note: the possessive is read as the plain word sides

explanation.surface: A team's grievances are not genuine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'phoney' rearranges sides, and the theme word SEA is then slotted in after the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Illnesses are commonly called complaints, as in a chest complaint.

clue.text: Extremely happy and sensible around animals

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
around here means turned round, so the word for sensible is written backwards

parts.note: sensible means sane, of sound mind

explanation.surface: Some creatures are both very cheerful and level-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' signals the turnaround. The animals are famous for a laughing call, which suits 'happy'.
explanation.definitionFit: These scavenging carnivores of Africa are animals, a plain example of the class.

clue.text: Eg Newcastle and Liverpool matches

definitions.meaning: both cities are seats of bishops, whose dioceses are so called
in poker one matches a bet by calling it, also said as seeing it

explanation.surface: Two English cities' football teams take on each other.
explanation.walkthrough: Newcastle and Liverpool look like football clubs and matches like fixtures; in fact they are bishoprics, and the poker verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop's diocese is formally called by this word, and in poker it means calls an equal stake.

clue.text: Singer may help her trace of Mancunian accent

parts.note: the preamble's three-letter word, absent from the wordplay and added to every themed answer

indicators.note: a trace is the smallest bit, so just the opening letter of Mancunian

parts.note: an accent on a syllable is stress

explanation.surface: A vocalist's Manchester twang shows through.
explanation.walkthrough: Singer is a brand of sewing machine, not a vocalist. A Mancunian is someone from Manchester; the theme word SEA starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who sews for a living would be helped by a Singer sewing machine.

clue.text: Key for Anglo-Saxon instrument

parts.note: a harp is a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: The key piece of an early English musical instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: This musical key, a semitone above A, is one of the keys a piece can be in.

clue.text: Short item about cold northern swimmer

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shortened word goes round the letter for cold
short means cut off, so the word for item loses its final letter

parts.note: an article is an item, as in an article of clothing
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: A brief newspaper piece concerns a polar animal in the chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' docks the item's last letter and 'about' wraps it round cold; the theme word SEA then goes before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A seal of polar waters is a marine mammal that swims in the far north.

clue.text: See surgeon in cosy armchair

a vet is an animal surgeon

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's theme word SEA, absent from the wordplay, goes before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This small sofa for two is a snug upholstered seat, close enough to an armchair.

clue.text: Sirenians frighten divers ultimately

explanation.walkthrough: Sirenians, named after the mythical sirens, are the order of manatees and dugongs; the theme word SEA opens the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Manatees and dugongs, the order Sirenia, are popularly known by this bovine name.

clue.text: Cable tackles Conservative know-all

indicators.note: to tackle here is to grab hold of, so the word for cable wraps round the letter

parts.note: a wire is a cable

explanation.surface: Vince Cable, a Liberal Democrat, takes on a smug Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: Vince Cable was a British Liberal Democrat politician, which misleads. The theme word SEA is slotted in after the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart aleck who thinks they know everything is called by this old term of scorn.

clue.text: Seamen set out across Spithead together

indicators.note: across means spanning, so the reordered letters go round the extra letter
set out means arranged afresh, so the letters of Seamen are reordered

parts.note: read as Spit head, the head of the word spit is its letter S

explanation.surface: Sailors leave together, crossing the Solent anchorage.
explanation.walkthrough: Spithead is a stretch of water off Portsmouth used as a naval anchorage; split as 'Spit head' it gives S, which ENMASE goes across.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means all as one body, a borrowed idiom for together.

clue.text: New candidate prefers this group to include a female

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble's theme word SEA, absent from the wordplay, goes before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh parliamentary hopeful would rather stand in a constituency their party is sure to hold.

clue.text: Work during conflict in Times shown on successive days?

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, so two of them give times

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so the word for work goes inside the conflict

parts.note: a war is a conflict
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A newspaper reports on wartime toil.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a drama screened in two episodes on consecutive days.
explanation.definitionFit: A serial split into two episodes may well be broadcast on consecutive days.

clue.text: Tea was brought back home inside cutter

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so the word for home goes into the charade

parts.note: cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the word was is read backwards

parts.note: in means at home

explanation.surface: Tea was carried back indoors to a woodcutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns was round, and 'inside' puts home between the tea and the turned word.
explanation.definitionFit: A powered saw with a toothed loop is a tool that cuts timber.

clue.text: What the Observer did, he did to the Listener

indicators.note: to a listener means as heard aloud, so the words are taken by sound

explanation.surface: A riddle set by one paper about what a rival magazine did.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer and The Listener look like publications, but they are just someone watching and someone hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone observing a warning takes notice of it, so observed means paid attention.

clue.text: Drive enemy back into grass

definitions.note: in golf, to make the first drive from the tee

indicators.note: into means placed inside, so the turned word goes within the grass

parts.note: tef, also spelt teff, is an Ethiopian cereal grass

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the word for enemy is written backwards

parts.note: a foe is an enemy

explanation.surface: A soldier pushes the foe back onto the turf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like motoring, but it is the opening golf shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving off from the first hole starts a golf round, the golfing phrase for that shot.

clue.text: Neckwear that's almost too risqué is banned

explanation.walkthrough: TO from 'almost' too, then RISQUE without IS gives RQUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A torc, a twisted metal collar of the ancient Celts, was worn round the neck.

clue.text: Catch embarrassed paparazzo

parts.note: embarrassment turns the face red
a paparazzo is a press photographer, one who snaps

explanation.surface: A celebrity photographer is caught out and blushes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' looks like a verb, but it is a fish caught by an angler.
explanation.definitionFit: This reddish food fish is a common catch for sea anglers.

clue.text: Spots rook on tree

clue.text: Painter appears in sombrero, usually
